title: Strait and narrow – assessing shipping chokepoints
gist: Oxford Economics argues the market's fixation on the Strait of Hormuz misses the roughly 30 major maritime chokepoints that carry global trade — with Malacca and Taiwan alone handling nearly a quarter of it. Two disruption drivers are highlighted: chokepoints being deliberately weaponised as political leverage, and climate/natural-disaster events already cutting Panama Canal draughts and shutting the world's busiest container ports.

themes.theme: Chokepoint concentration is broader than Hormuz

insights.claim: Analysis of shipping risk that focuses on the Strait of Hormuz is too narrow, because Hormuz is only one of many global chokepoints, each with different vulnerabilities and differing importance to global, regional, and economy-specific trade.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Hedging shipping/geopolitical risk purely through Gulf-linked oil and freight exposure leaves the bulk of chokepoint risk unhedged; map exposure across the full set of passages.
insights.quote: But the Strait of Hormuz is just one of many global shipping chokepoints.
insights.locator: Recent analysis on the implications for global shipping

insights.claim: There are around 30 major maritime chokepoints that matter for global trade, most of which are not household names.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Sets the scope for a supply-chain risk screen: roughly 30 passages, not the two or three that make headlines.
insights.quote: There are around 30 major chokepoints that matter for global trade.

insights.claim: Almost one-quarter of global trade passes through the Malacca and Taiwan Straits.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Concentration of this scale means an Asian chokepoint incident would be a far larger global trade shock than a Gulf event; watch shipping rates and Asia-exposed freight names.
insights.quote: almost one-quarter of global trade passes through the Malacca and Taiwan Straits
insights.locator: The volume moving through these passages is massive

insights.claim: The nature of geopolitical chokepoint risk is shifting: passages are increasingly treated as instruments of leverage — assets to be controlled, taxed, or threatened — rather than as accidents of geography.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Implies chokepoint disruption becomes a recurring policy tool rather than a tail event, raising the structural floor under freight rates, insurance costs, and rerouting expense.
insights.quote: Chokepoints are increasingly treated as instruments of leverage rather than accidents of geography – assets to be controlled, taxed, or threatened.
insights.locator: Two forces stand out as potential catalysts

insights.claim: The short-lived nature of June's memorandum of understanding and continuing Houthi rebel actions in the Red Sea point to a bumpy path toward any reopening, with progress over the remainder of the year expected to follow a pattern of one step forward, two steps back.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Argues against pricing a clean normalisation trade in Red Sea shipping; expect repeated false dawns and reversals through year-end.
insights.quote: We expect progress through the remainder of the year to follow a pattern of one step forward, two steps back.
insights.locator: Assessments of the likelihood of another deal

themes.theme: Climate and natural disasters as a second disruption driver

insights.claim: Natural disasters and climate are identified as the second major potential driver of chokepoint disruption, alongside geopolitics.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Chokepoint risk models built only on conflict scenarios understate frequency; weather-driven closures are already recurring.
insights.locator: The second potential driver of chokepoint disruption

insights.claim: The Panama Canal has cut vessel draughts five times this year as El Niño threatens to drain its water supply.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Draught restrictions cut effective canal capacity per vessel — a live, measurable cost input for transpacific and Atlantic routing.
insights.quote: The Panama Canal has cut vessel draughts five times this year as El Niño threatens to drain its water supply
insights.locator: The second potential driver of chokepoint disruption

insights.claim: Typhoons have twice shut the world's busiest container ports within a single month.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Weather closures at top-tier ports are frequent enough to matter for quarterly logistics costs and delivery schedules, not just tail-risk planning.
insights.quote: typhoons have twice shut the world’s busiest container ports in a month
insights.locator: The second potential driver of chokepoint disruption

themes.theme: Transport risk versus concentration risk for firms

insights.claim: Diversifying suppliers is insufficient if the goods still travel the same routes, so transport risk must be assessed alongside supplier concentration risk.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A useful due-diligence lens: companies claiming diversified sourcing may still carry single-chokepoint exposure — probe routing, not just supplier lists.
insights.quote: diversifying suppliers isn’t enough if the goods still travel the same routes; transport risk needs assessing alongside concentration risk
